core: Definition of phishing as a social attack: fraudulent messages posing as trusted senders to trick recipients into revealing information or clicking harmful links
How phishing works conceptually: fake urgency, impersonation of trusted senders, fake login pages
Common types: email phishing, smishing (SMS), vishing (voice calls), spear phishing (targeted)
Red flags: unexpected urgency, unfamiliar sender, mismatched links, requests for credentials or payments, poor grammar (with AI-era caveat)
What to do when suspicious: don't click, don't reply, report, verify through another channel
Why phishing succeeds: it exploits trust and emotion, not just ignorance
Multi-factor authentication as a damage-limiting layer
Role of security-awareness training (referenced only; sibling topic)
supporting: Phishing is a significant and widespread threat (time-anchored to cited sources)
AI-generated messages can have perfect grammar, making grammar an unreliable standalone sign
outOfScope: Social engineering as the broader category (own topic: cybersecurity:foundations:social-engineering)
Malware and its delivery mechanics (own topic: cybersecurity:foundations:malware)
Step-by-step attack techniques, exploit details, or offensive tooling

claims.claim: Phishing is a form of social engineering in which fraudulent messages or websites pose as a trusted person or organization to trick people into revealing personal or financial information or clicking harmful links.
Phishing typically works through fake urgency, impersonation of trusted senders, and fake login pages that capture credentials.
The common forms of phishing are email phishing (most common), smishing (SMS/text messages), vishing (voice calls), and spear phishing (targeted at specific people based on research).

Common red flags include unexpected urgency, unfamiliar senders, mismatched links, requests for credentials or payments, and poor grammar — with the caveat that AI-generated messages may have perfect grammar and spelling.

The recommended response to a suspected phishing message is to not click links or attachments, not reply, report the message, and verify through an independent channel (a known website or phone number, never the contact information inside the message).
Phishing succeeds by exploiting trust and emotion — urgency, fear, and familiarity — rather than mere ignorance, and even careful people can be deceived.

Phishing is a significant and widespread threat: the FTC reports that scammers launch thousands of phishing attacks every day, and NIST's authentication guidance calls phishing a significant threat vector.

Multi-factor authentication limits the damage of a phished password; NIST guidance notes that passwords alone are not phishing-resistant and encourages phishing-resistant authentication options where practical.
Security-awareness training helps people recognize and report phishing attempts; the topic of security-awareness is covered in its own lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether poor grammar is a reliable phishing indicator
positions: CISA (Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks) and Microsoft both list poor grammar, misspellings, and awkward wording among common phishing indicators.
CISA (Recognize and Report Phishing) notes that in the era of AI, some phishing messages now have perfect grammar and spelling, so grammar alone is no longer reliable.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson lists poor grammar among the red flags but explicitly carries CISA's caveat that AI-era messages can be flawless, directing readers to weight urgency, sender address, and link destinations more heavily.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where a user should report a suspected phishing message
positions: FTC consumer guidance: forward phishing emails to the Anti-Phishing Working Group and texts to the SPAM short code, and file a report with the FTC.
Microsoft: report through your organization's IT department or designated reporting tools.
CISA: use the report option near the sender's address or the 'report spam' button in the mail client.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps reporting advice general — 'use the report option in your email or messaging app, and consumer agencies such as the FTC also accept reports' — a statement all three sources support, without prescribing one channel over another.
